strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computational pathology problem: obtaining reusable representations for image–text retrieval, patch classification, and queries combining images and questions. PMEB could provide a useful common evaluation framework for these capabilities.

The reported improvements are substantial and reasonably broad. For example, MLLM4PUE-P improves Arch-PubMed image-to-text Recall@5 from PathCLIP’s 0.275 to 0.372, and classification weighted F1 from 0.492 to 0.783 on Kather7k and from 0.267 to 0.502 on Sicap. Testing adaptation on three pathology training sources strengthens the empirical case.

The fusion ablation provides useful evidence for processing images and questions jointly: on Quilt-VQA-RED, prompted fusion achieves Recall@5 of 0.675 versus 0.520 for embedding addition and 0.429 for questions alone.

The approach is straightforward and technically plausible, combining a pretrained MLLM, last-token representations, contrastive alignment, and parameter-efficient adaptation. The manuscript provides several implementation settings and investigates the effect of benchmark subsampling.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General category, the methodological advance over E5-V is limited. The summarization prompt and last-token embedding strategy closely follow that work, while pathology image–text contrastive training and QLoRA are established components. Comparing against E5-V without pathology adaptation does not isolate the proposed contribution. A controlled comparison using the same backbone and adaptation data, together with prompt/pooling ablations, is needed to establish what is gained beyond domain fine-tuning.

The zero-shot evaluation lacks a documented training–test overlap audit. Training sources aggregate public pathology material, while evaluation includes textbook/article images and Quilt-derived VQA data. The supplied manuscript does not establish separation at image, article, or source-video level. This does not demonstrate contamination, but it leaves an important uncertainty, particularly because Quilt-trained MLLM4PUE-Q obtains much larger composed-retrieval gains than the other variants.

PMEB’s construction is insufficiently specified for a central benchmark contribution. ChatGPT-based cleaning is described without prompts, model version, validation, or precise filtering rules. Candidate-answer construction, treatment of duplicate or semantically equivalent answers, fixed sample identifiers, and sampling seeds are unclear. These choices directly affect retrieval difficulty and reproducibility. The referenced supplementary material is not included in the supplied manuscript.

The comparisons do not adequately separate architecture, pretraining, data preparation, and compute. An 8B pretrained MLLM has substantially different prior training and capacity from the CLIP baselines; sharing a named pathology dataset does not control these factors. Openpath is reconstructed and Quilt captions are concatenated, but identical baseline training inputs and retraining procedures are not established. CONCH is omitted from retrieval evaluations. Claims of data efficiency based only on pathology adaptation-pair counts therefore need qualification.

Important reproducibility and uncertainty information is missing: training duration, LoRA rank and target modules, optimizer/schedule details, exact checkpoint, and an unambiguous definition of the extracted token state. No confidence intervals or repeated sampling/training runs are reported. The acknowledged 0.01–0.04 variation with benchmark size is comparable to several reported gains, so subsampling experiments alone do not establish stable model rankings.

The broader claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Evaluation covers patch classification and retrieval, without testing whole-slide tasks or the claimed benefit of longer textual context. No inference latency, memory, or embedding-storage comparison establishes the practical cost of replacing compact encoders with an 8B MLLM. Smaller modality-centroid gaps and t-SNE clusters also do not independently establish better semantic alignment.

Several presentation and attribution errors should be corrected: the abstract reports 16 tasks from 15 datasets, whereas Section 3 and Table 1 report 15 from 14; Databiox is labeled as colorectal cancer and cites the CRC-100k reference; and some table references are incorrect. These are secondary to the experimental concerns, but weaken confidence in the benchmark documentation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: reusable pathology representations supporting image–text retrieval, tissue classification, and queries combining images with questions. PMEB could provide a useful common evaluation framework.

The reported improvements are substantial and span three pathology training sources. For example, MLLM4PUE-P improves Arch-PubMed image-to-text Recall@5 from PathCLIP’s 0.275 to 0.372, and improves classification wF1 from 0.611 to 0.763 on CRC-100k and from 0.492 to 0.783 on Kather7k.

Table 5 provides useful within-model evidence for joint image–question processing: prompt-based fusion improves Recall@5 over embedding addition from 0.394 to 0.475 on Quilt-VQA and from 0.520 to 0.675 on Quilt-VQA-RED.

The framework is straightforward, and the manuscript identifies its backbone, training sources, basic optimization settings, and evaluation prompts. The sample-size ablation also makes a useful initial attempt to justify a computationally manageable benchmark.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the methodological advance is limited and insufficiently isolated. Summarization prompting and last-token embeddings closely follow the cited E5-V approach; the adaptation principally adds pathology image–text contrastive training and QLoRA. Comparing against E5-V without pathology adaptation does not establish an advantage over a comparably adapted predecessor. The claim that E5-V requires a pathology instruction-pretrained LLM is not substantiated.

The zero-shot evaluation needs a documented training–test overlap audit. Training sources aggregate public pathology material, while evaluation uses textbook/PubMed content and Quilt-derived VQA. No image, caption, or source-level disjointness checks are reported. This does not establish contamination, but leaves an important uncertainty, especially because Quilt-trained MLLM4PUE substantially outperforms the other training variants on Quilt-VQA.

PMEB’s central reproducibility claim is not adequately supported in the supplied manuscript. The ChatGPT cleaning procedure lacks prompts, model/version information, explicit filtering rules, and validation of retained answers. Composed retrieval also needs a precise candidate-pool definition and handling of duplicate or semantically equivalent answers. Sampling identifiers/seeds and an accessible benchmark release are not provided; the referenced supplementary details are not included in the supplied PDF.

The comparisons do not disentangle architecture, prior pretraining, and adaptation. An 8B MLLM has substantially different capacity and pretraining from the CLIP-based baselines, and matching the pathology dataset source does not control these factors. An unadapted same-backbone baseline and controlled adaptation/pooling comparisons would clarify the contribution. Claims of data efficiency count pathology adaptation pairs without accounting for prior pretraining, while inference cost and embedding-storage requirements are unreported.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Table 5 demonstrates that images help, but does not establish that the benchmark requires genuine visual reasoning; shuffled-image controls would better test this, particularly given the substantial question-only scores. Similarly, smaller modality-centroid gaps and tighter t-SNE clusters do not independently demonstrate better semantic alignment. The claimed long-text advantage is not directly evaluated.

Benchmark reliability and reporting require improvement. No confidence intervals or repeated sampling results are given, and the reported 0.01–0.04 variation with sample size can matter for close model rankings. The abstract states 16 tasks from 15 datasets, whereas Table 1 and the main text state 15 from 14. Table 1 also cites the colorectal dataset reference for Databiox, and several table references are incorrect. These editorial issues are individually repairable, but reinforce uncertainty about the benchmark specification. Training duration, LoRA configuration, and the precise hidden-state extraction convention are also missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: reusable pathology embeddings supporting image–text retrieval, patch classification, and joint image–question queries. PMEB offers a potentially valuable common evaluation framework.

The reported improvements are broad and often substantial. For example, MLLM4PUE-P improves Arch-PubMed image-to-text Recall@5 from 0.275 to 0.372 over PathCLIP, and classification weighted F1 from 0.492 to 0.783 on Kather7k. Evaluating adaptations on three pathology training sources strengthens the empirical case.

The within-model fusion ablation provides meaningful evidence for joint multimodal encoding. On Quilt-VQA, prompt-based fusion improves Recall@5 from 0.394 with embedding addition to 0.475; on Quilt-VQA-RED, it improves from 0.520 to 0.675.
The method is straightforward and technically plausible. The sampling-size study and quantitative modality-gap measurements provide useful supporting analyses beyond the main performance tables.
weaknesses: The methodological advance over E5-V is insufficiently established. Summarization prompts and last-token embeddings closely follow that cited approach, with pathology image–text contrastive adaptation providing the main change. E5-V is evaluated without pathology adaptation, and there is no controlled comparison using the same backbone, training data, and alternative embedding extraction strategies. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, this leaves the distinct technical contribution and source of improvement unclear.

The zero-shot evaluation needs a documented training–test overlap audit. Training uses aggregated public pathology sources, while evaluation includes textbook/PubMed imagery and Quilt-derived VQA data. The manuscript does not establish source-level separation or describe deduplication against evaluation sets. This is particularly consequential for the large gains of the Quilt1M-trained model on Quilt-VQA; overlap is not demonstrated, but independence is not established either.

PMEB is not specified sufficiently to reproduce its central composed-retrieval evaluation from the supplied manuscript. Candidate-answer pool construction, duplicate or semantically equivalent answers, relevance judgments, and the ChatGPT cleaning prompts and validation procedure are unclear. Dataset details are deferred to supplementary material that was not supplied. Question-only comparisons show that images help, but do not establish the stronger claim that shortcuts have been eliminated.

The comparisons do not isolate architecture, model scale, or prior pretraining from the proposed adaptation. An 8B MLLM has substantially different resources from the CLIP-based baselines, and matching the pathology source does not match total training exposure. Consequently, the data-efficiency claims need qualification. Inference latency, memory, and embedding-storage costs are also missing despite the motivation of sustainable, reusable representations.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement: training duration, LoRA configuration, precise checkpoint identity, sampling seeds, and uncertainty estimates are not provided. The benchmark is described as 16 tasks from 15 datasets in the abstract but 15 tasks from 14 datasets elsewhere, and Table 1 attributes Databiox to the CRC-100k reference. These reporting corrections are individually secondary, but the missing controls and evaluation provenance leave the overall evidence slightly short of acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: pathology retrieval with queries containing multiple images, text, or video. The PCR benchmark provides a potentially useful evaluation direction beyond conventional image–text retrieval.

The reported composed-retrieval gains are substantial. In Table 2, HOMIE achieves 78.5% R@1 on multi-image-to-text retrieval versus 44.3% for the strongest baseline, and improves performance across all five evaluated composed-retrieval settings.

Evaluation extends to four conventional retrieval datasets and nine tile-classification datasets. HOMIE remains competitive on conventional retrieval and matches or exceeds the reported classification baselines on eight of nine datasets, suggesting useful transfer beyond the proposed task.

The framework uses public training data and integrates established techniques coherently. Tables 5–6 provide useful evidence for curriculum training, native-resolution processing, data filtering, and joint query encoding; removing curriculum training reduces average composed R@1 from 53.2% to 47.4%.
weaknesses: The benchmark's validity is insufficiently established. Section 3.1 uses GPT-5 to generate relational queries and rewrite VQA answers, but the supplied manuscript reports no expert validation, annotation agreement, or error analysis. Answer paraphrasing does not establish that retrieval requires visual grounding. Image-only, text-only, shuffled-image, and single-frame controls are needed to distinguish genuine composition and temporal understanding from shortcuts. Candidate-pool construction and treatment of multiple valid answers also remain unclear.

The zero-shot claims lack a documented contamination audit. HOMIE trains on aggregated PathGen, PathCap, and Quilt data, while evaluation repurposes public textbook, publication, and educational-video datasets. The manuscript does not establish separation through image, source-document, video, or patient-level deduplication. This does not demonstrate leakage, but leaves an important uncertainty. Section 4.2's suggestion that CONCH's stronger Pubmedset results arise from overlap is likewise unsupported by an audit.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed adaptation framework from domain training and backbone capability. General MLLM retrieval baselines are evaluated without matched pathology adaptation, and there is no same-backbone baseline trained on the same data with a standard retrieval recipe. Crucially, Table 5 never removes Stage 1, despite the two-stage design being central to the claimed contribution. The experiments therefore do not establish how much improvement specifically comes from resolving the proposed task mismatch.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Removing stain normalization/augmentation changes composed R@1 only from 53.2% to 53.1%, contradicting claims that this component is essential. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates support the small classification gains or ablation differences. Similarly, a lower modality-gap score and UMAP visualization do not prove correct semantic alignment. The video comparison also excludes pathology encoders rather than testing a straightforward frame-pooling baseline.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Important missing details include the filtering threshold and bootstrap-model configuration, LoRA settings, contrastive temperature, video frame sampling, image-resolution limits, and precise benchmark-generation and classification prompts. Section 3.3 describes tuning the entire MLLM, whereas the implementation specifies the vision encoder, projector, and LLM LoRA modules. The referenced supplementary material is not included in the supplied PDF.

Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, methodological originality is primarily the pathology-specific integration of existing MLLM embedding, curriculum, filtering, and stain-processing techniques. This could support acceptance through a convincing benchmark and controlled empirical evidence, without requiring a new architecture. However, the unresolved benchmark-validity and experimental-control concerns currently weaken that case enough to favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile computer-vision problem: pathology retrieval with queries combining images and text. The PCR benchmark brings together multi-image, image–text, and video retrieval tasks, extending evaluation beyond conventional image–caption matching.

The reported improvements are substantial. In Table 2, HOMIE achieves 78.5% R@1 on multi-image retrieval versus 44.3% for the strongest baseline, and 30.7% on video retrieval versus 5.3%. Tables 3–4 also show competitive conventional retrieval and tile classification, suggesting that specialization does not sacrifice these capabilities.

The framework combines public training resources with a coherent adaptation strategy. Table 5 supports the usefulness of data filtering, curriculum ordering, and native-resolution processing; Table 6 provides evidence that joint prompting improves over addition of separately computed embeddings.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not adequately isolate the methodological contribution. HOMIE receives substantial pathology-specific training, whereas the general MLLM retrieval baselines remain general-domain models. A same-backbone retrieval baseline trained on the same pathology data is needed to distinguish the proposed framework from ordinary domain adaptation. Table 5 does not ablate Stage 1, despite the central claim that the two-stage design resolves distinct mismatches. The familiar ingredients can form a valuable contribution, but their incremental benefit over a straightforward adaptation is insufficiently established.

The new benchmark needs stronger validation. Section 3.1 uses GPT-5 to generate relational queries and rewrite VQA answers, but reports no expert verification, annotation-error analysis, or image-only/text-only controls. Rephrasing answers does not establish that retrieving them requires visual evidence. Candidate-pool construction, handling of multiple valid answers, and source-level separation also need clarification. These omissions directly affect whether PCR measures the claimed compositional reasoning.

Training–evaluation independence is insufficiently documented. Training uses Quilt-1M and evaluation uses Quilt-VQA/Quilt-VQA-RED, yet the supplied manuscript provides no source-video or image-level overlap audit. This is a risk requiring verification, not evidence that contamination occurred. Conversely, Section 4.2 attributes CONCH’s stronger Pubmedset results to probable training overlap without substantiating that explanation; using public training data does not itself establish HOMIE’s independence.

The baseline protocol makes architectural claims stronger than the evidence supports. Restricting pathology encoders to embedding addition is a useful baseline, but does not establish that alternative fusion is inapplicable or that these architectures fundamentally fail. In particular, video retrieval omits frame-pooling baselines despite their requiring no video-specific training. Frame-order and single-frame controls would also help establish whether HOMIE exploits temporal information.

Several interpretations exceed the measurements. Removing stain normalization/augmentation changes composed R@1 only from 53.2 to 53.1 in Table 5, which does not support calling it essential without uncertainty estimates. Curriculum versus mixed-data training does not establish that morphology must precede diagnostic learning without reverse-order and exposure-matched controls. Likewise, a smaller global modality gap and UMAP mixing do not prove semantic correspondence. No repeated-run or confidence-interval evidence is given.

Reproducibility and practical scope remain incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Important details include the filtering threshold and bootstrap model, LoRA configuration, image-token/resolution limits, video sampling, and exact curriculum schedule. Some details are deferred to supplementary material that is not supplied. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent despite the 7B backbone and large-database motivation. These gaps, together with the benchmark and comparison concerns, outweigh the promising reported gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: retrieving pathology evidence using queries that combine images and text. The PCR benchmark extends evaluation beyond conventional image–text retrieval to multi-image, relational, VQA-derived, and video queries.

The reported composed-retrieval gains are substantial. In Table 2, HOMIE achieves 78.5% multi-image-to-text R@1 versus 44.3% for the strongest baseline, and 64.3% on Quilt-VQA-RED versus 52.4%. Improvements occur across all five evaluated settings.

Evaluation covers complementary capabilities: composed retrieval, bidirectional simple retrieval, and nine tile-classification datasets. HOMIE remains competitive on conventional tasks, suggesting that compositional adaptation does not sacrifice useful pathology representations.

The framework combines established techniques coherently and uses public training datasets. Ablations support the usefulness of curriculum training and native-resolution processing, while Table 6 provides evidence that joint encoding improves over embedding addition.
weaknesses: The benchmark's validity is insufficiently established. Section 3.1 uses GPT-5 to generate relational queries and rewrite VQA answers, but the supplied manuscript reports no expert verification, annotation error analysis, or treatment of multiple clinically equivalent answers. Rephrasing answers does not establish that retrieval requires visual grounding; image-only, text-only, and shuffled-image controls are needed to substantiate the central compositional-reasoning claim.

Training–evaluation independence is not adequately documented. Training includes Quilt-1M and PathCap, while evaluation draws on related pathology video, publication, and educational sources. No source-level separation or duplicate/near-duplicate audit is reported. This does not establish contamination, but leaves the zero-shot claims uncertain. Conversely, Section 4.2 attributes CONCH's Pubmedset advantage to probable overlap without presenting supporting evidence.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution of the proposed adaptation framework. General retrieval MLLMs are evaluated without matched pathology adaptation, whereas HOMIE receives substantial domain-specific training. A same-backbone, same-data direct fine-tuning baseline and an ablation removing Stage 1 are particularly important. The current results cannot establish the claimed necessity of the two-stage design.

Baseline restrictions weaken the architectural conclusions. CLIP-based models use only simple embedding addition, without investigating normalized or weighted fusion, and are excluded from video evaluation even though frame-level encoding and pooling would provide a feasible baseline. Their results therefore do not demonstrate an inherent inability to handle these tasks.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the supplied manuscript, which refers to an unavailable supplement. Missing information includes filtering threshold and selection procedure, LoRA configuration, image-token/resolution limits, video sampling, and precise candidate-pool and relevance construction. Section 3.3 also describes fine-tuning the entire MLLM, whereas implementation details specify vision/projector training plus LLM LoRA.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Removing stain processing changes composed R@1 only from 53.2 to 53.1, contradicting claims that every component is essential. Small classification improvements lack uncertainty estimates, and reduced modality gap does not prove semantic correctness. With no declared contribution type, I assess this as Algorithms/General: the practical integration is promising, but its largely established ingredients make the unresolved benchmark and controlled-comparison issues consequential enough to favor rejection.
